about: Curated NASA Earth-science variable catalog for the 2026 Space Apps challenge 'Be An Earth System Trend Detective!'. Built 2026-11-12 from live probes of each API. Identifiers were checked against the live services that day. 'plain' is the student-friendly definition. 'good_for' lists region types the variable is likely to show trends in (drives variable suggestions).

power.name: NASA POWER (Prediction Of Worldwide Energy Resources)
power.limits: Regional box must span 2-10 degrees in BOTH lat and lon (else HTTP 422). Grid 0.5 x 0.625 deg. Monthly ends at last full year (2025). Key 'YYYY13' = annual value, drop it. Fill value -999.
power.cite: NASA Langley Research Center POWER Project, funded through the NASA Earth Science/Applied Science Program

giovanni_ts.name: GES DISC Giovanni in the Cloud - Time Series Service (point)
giovanni_ts.limits: Single point only. Monthly compute quota per user: GET https://api.giovanni.earthdata.nasa.gov/quota returns 0..1 used.
giovanni_ts.verified: 2026-11-12: GPM_3IMERGM_07_precipitation point series OK. IMERG Final monthly lags ~3 months (ended 2025-09).

giovanni_area.name: Giovanni Area-Averaged Time Series via NASA Harmony
giovanni_area.how: harmony-py: Request(collection=Collection(id=<CMR concept id>), spatial=BBox(w,s,e,n), temporal={start,stop}, variables=['<giovanni var id>'], format='text/csv', average='area')
giovanni_area.returns: CSV with header attrs then time,mean_<var>
giovanni_area.limits: Async job (seconds-minutes). Shares the Giovanni quota. Same variable ids as giovanni_ts.
giovanni_area.verified: 2026-11-12: GPM_3IMERGM 2000-2025 over a 10x3 deg box returned in 34 s. Collection concept id for GPM_3IMERGM v07 = C2723754851-GES_DISC (look others up via CMR).

opendap.name: Earthdata Cloud OPeNDAP (Hyrax) - server-side subsetting of any GES DISC file
opendap.auth: Earthdata token + 'NASA GESDISC DATA ARCHIVE' app approved
opendap.limits: One request per file (per month for monthly products). Get granule URLs from CMR - the MERRA-2 stream number (100/200/300/400/401) varies. Values >1e10 are fill. .dmr lists dimensions.

appeears.name: AppEEARS (LP DAAC) - MODIS / VIIRS / SMAP / Landsat / ECOSTRESS
appeears.auth: Own token: POST /api/login with Earthdata username:password (Basic auth) -> bearer token valid ~48 h. The Earthdata user token is REJECTED (403, verified 2026-11-12). Product + layer listing is public.
appeears.how: POST /task {task_type:'area', geo: GeoJSON polygon, layers:[{product, layer}], output:{format:{type:'netcdf4'}, projection:'geographic'}} -> poll /status -> /bundle; the bundle includes a <product>-Statistics.csv (mean/median/std per date over the polygon).
appeears.limits: Async, minutes to an hour for long MODIS records. Precompute demo regions. 193 products.

cmr.name: Common Metadata Repository (the engine behind Earthdata Search)

gibs.name: GIBS imagery tiles (the engine behind Worldview)

nsidc_seaice.name: NSIDC Sea Ice Index G02135 (NASA DAAC)
nsidc_seaice.maps: https://noaadata.apps.nsidc.org/NOAA/G02135/{north|south}/monthly/geotiff/{MM}_{Mon}/{N|S}_{YYYYMM}_concentration_v4.0.tif (~0.67 MB, polar stereographic; v3.0 names are gone = 404)
nsidc_seaice.notes: Monthly extent + area, 1978-present, one consistent record. Sep 2026 Arctic extent 4.81 M km2. Use the maps for time-lapse frames so the picture matches the number.

podaac.name: PO.DAAC (ocean + GRACE) files in Earthdata Cloud
podaac.auth: Earthdata token as Bearer header - works directly, no extra app approval (verified 2026-11-12)
podaac.notes: Small text files (sea level, ice mass) are a few KB-150 KB. GRACE grid = one 44 MB netCDF with every month.

veda.name: NASA VEDA / Earth Information Center STAC + raster API
veda.notes: 247 collections, mostly event snapshots. Useful long series: fldas-soil-moisture-anomalies (1982-2023 monthly), MODIS_Terra_L3_NDVI_16Day, no2-monthly (2016-2022), OMI_trno2-COG (annual 2005-2022).

variables.name: Air temperature (2 m)
variables.plain: How warm the air is about head-height above the ground, averaged over the month.

story.name: Air temperature
story.why: This is the temperature people, crops and animals actually feel. For scale: the whole planet has warmed by just over 1 °C since the late 1800s, and that alone has made once-a-decade heat extremes nearly three times as common.
story.up: Warmer air brings more frequent and stronger heatwaves, which are dangerous for health, especially for older people and outdoor workers. It also stresses crops and dries soils faster.
story.down: Cooler air can mean more frost and a shorter growing season. Local cooling can also come from more cloud, haze or irrigation.

variables.name: Air temperature by altitude (pressure level)
variables.plain: Temperature at different heights in the atmosphere - from near the ground up into the stratosphere (where the ozone layer is). Lower air is warming while the high air is cooling.

look.note: The map shows the 250 hPa level (~10 km up).

variables.demo: Global 1980-2025: 850 hPa +0.20, 500 hPa +0.23, 50 hPa -0.30 K/decade (all p<1e-7). Antarctic 50 hPa -0.58 K/decade (ozone hole). 1 hPa has an observing-system jump ~1999-2005: use 2005+ only (-0.99 K/decade).
variables.notes: Below-ground cells are 1e15 fill (mask). Other 3-D vars in the same file: U, V, QV (humidity), O3, H (height), RH, OMEGA.

variables.name: Daily maximum temperature (monthly average)
variables.plain: The hottest point of the day (usually afternoon), averaged over the month.

story.name: Daytime high temperature
story.why: The hottest part of each day, averaged over the month. This is what drives heat stress for people, animals and crops.
story.up: Hotter afternoons mean more dangerous heat for outdoor work, more electricity for cooling, and lower harvests of heat-sensitive crops such as wheat and maize.
story.down: Cooler afternoons ease heat stress. They can come from more cloud, rain or irrigation.

look.note: The map shows monthly mean air temperature.

variables.demo: Delhi region (27.5-29.5N, 76-78E): -0.31 degC/decade, p=0.002 - afternoons COOLING under haze

variables.name: Daily minimum temperature (monthly average)
variables.plain: The coolest point of the day (usually just before sunrise). Cities and humid air keep nights warm.

story.name: Night-time low temperature
story.why: The coolest part of each day, usually at night. Cool nights matter because people and plants recover from daytime heat while it is cool.
story.up: Warmer nights give people less relief during heatwaves, can lower rice harvests, mean fewer frosts, and let some pests survive the winter.
story.down: Colder nights bring more frost, which can damage crops and early blossoms.

look.note: The map shows monthly mean air temperature.

variables.name: Hot days (35 °C or more)
variables.plain: How many days each year the afternoon air reaches 35 °C or more.

story.name: Hot days (35 °C+)
story.why: Counting extreme days says more about danger than an average does: a small rise in the average can mean many more scorching days.
story.up: More 35 °C days mean more heat stroke risk, lost outdoor work hours, crop damage and higher power demand for cooling.
story.down: Fewer extreme days ease heat stress, though humid heat can still be dangerous below 35 °C.

access.source: NASA POWER daily maximum air temperature (MERRA-2), counted per year

variables.name: Humid-heat days (wet-bulb 26 °C+)
variables.plain: How many days each year are so hot AND humid that sweat stops cooling the body well: the wet-bulb temperature averages 26 °C or more.

story.name: Humid-heat days
story.why: Wet-bulb temperature combines heat and humidity. It is what a thermometer wrapped in a wet cloth reads, and it tells how well sweating can cool you. Near 35 °C wet-bulb, even a healthy person in the shade cannot survive for long.
story.up: More humid-heat days mean more dangerous days for outdoor workers, farmers and older people, even when the thermometer does not look extreme.
story.down: Fewer humid-heat days mean the body can cool itself more easily.

access.source: NASA POWER daily wet-bulb temperature (MERRA-2), counted per year

variables.name: Land surface temperature (MODIS, day)
variables.plain: How hot the ground itself is in the daytime, measured by the MODIS satellite camera at 1 km - streets, fields and forests each show their own heat.

story.name: Daytime ground temperature
story.why: Satellites see how hot the ground gets by day. Cities, bare soil and cleared forest heat up much more than green fields or water.
story.up: Hotter ground by day often means fewer trees, more concrete or drier soil, and it makes heatwaves feel worse.
story.down: Cooler ground can mean more plants, wetter soil or more cloud.

access.source: MODIS Terra MOD11A2 v061 (1 km, 8-day) via ORNL DAAC, no login

variables.name: Ocean chlorophyll (plankton)
variables.plain: How green the sea is: chlorophyll from tiny floating plants (phytoplankton), the base of the ocean food web. Near river mouths, mud and river water also colour the sea.

story.name: Ocean chlorophyll
story.why: Phytoplankton feed almost all sea life. Near big rivers the colour also shows what the river carries: mud, nutrients and fertiliser (Acker et al. 2009, NASA).
story.up: More chlorophyll can mean more nutrients washing in from farms and cities, which can lead to algal blooms and low-oxygen dead zones.
story.down: Less chlorophyll can mean warmer, more layered water bringing up fewer nutrients, or less sediment from dammed rivers.

access.source: MODIS Aqua yearly chlorophyll-a, 9 km (OB.DAAC R2022.0), doi:10.5067/AQUA/MODIS/L3M/CHL/2022

variables.notes: Precomputed: scripts in app/build_chl.py average each yearly 9 km map onto a 0.25 deg grid; any ocean box then averages those cells (log-mean, as in Acker et al. 2009).

variables.name: Surface (skin) temperature
variables.plain: How hot the ground, plants or sea surface themselves are - what a thermal camera would see. Over the ocean this is sea surface temperature.

story.name: Ground surface temperature
story.why: How hot the ground or sea surface itself is. On a sunny day it can be much hotter than the air.
story.up: A hotter surface dries soil faster and adds to city heat. Over the sea, warmer water can fuel stronger storms and bleach coral reefs.
story.down: A cooler surface can mean more cloud, snow or moisture at the ground.

variables.name: Relative humidity (2 m)
variables.plain: How close the air is to being saturated with water vapour. High humidity makes heat feel worse.

story.name: Humidity
story.why: How close the air is to holding all the water it can. Heat feels much worse in humid air because sweat cannot evaporate to cool you.
story.up: More humid air makes heatwaves more dangerous to health and helps mould and some crop diseases spread.
story.down: Drier air pulls water out of plants and soil faster and raises wildfire risk.

look.note: The map is AIRS satellite humidity; the numbers are MERRA-2 (via POWER).

variables.name: Total column water vapour
variables.plain: All the invisible water vapour in the air above a spot, stacked up. Warmer air holds more.

story.name: Water vapour in the air
story.why: All the water vapour in the air above a spot, in kilograms over each square metre. Warmer air can hold about 7% more water for every 1 °C, and that extra water feeds heavier downpours.
story.up: More water vapour means heavier rain when storms hit. Water vapour also traps heat, so it adds to warming.
story.down: Less water vapour means drier air and usually less rain.

variables.name: Sunlight reaching the ground
variables.plain: How much solar energy actually reaches the surface after clouds and haze block some of it.

story.name: Sunlight reaching the ground
story.why: How much of the Sun's energy reaches the ground each day. It powers plant growth and solar panels, and it changes when clouds or haze change.
story.up: More sunlight usually means fewer clouds or cleaner air. It helps solar power and plants but adds to heat and drought stress.
story.down: Less sunlight usually means more cloud or haze from air pollution. A long decline like this is called 'dimming'.

look.note: The map shows sunlight over land only.

variables.demo: Delhi pre-monsoon (Apr-Jun): -0.39 MJ/m2/day per decade, p=3e-5 ('dimming')

variables.name: Cloud cover
variables.plain: The share of the sky covered by clouds.

story.name: Cloud cover
story.why: How much of the sky is covered by cloud. Clouds shade the ground by day and hold heat in at night.
story.up: More cloud usually means less sunshine at the ground, cooler days, warmer nights and often more rain.
story.down: Less cloud lets more sunshine through, which can make days hotter and dry out soils faster.

look.note: The map shows how bright the clouds are (cloud albedo); the numbers show cloud amount.

variables.name: Wind speed (10 m)
variables.plain: How fast the wind blows 10 m above the ground.

story.name: Wind speed
story.why: Average wind speed 10 m above the ground. It matters for wind power, dust storms, waves, and how quickly heat and air pollution blow away.
story.up: Stronger winds can lift more dust, build bigger waves and produce more wind power.
story.down: Weaker winds let heat and air pollution build up, and wind turbines produce less power.

variables.name: Precipitation (rain + snow)
variables.plain: How much rain and snow falls, as an average depth per day.

story.name: Rain and snow
story.why: How much water falls from the sky, in millimetres per day (1 mm on 1 m² is 1 litre). It is the main water supply for farms, rivers and drinking water.
story.up: More rain can mean more floods and landslides, but also more water for crops and reservoirs.
story.down: Less rain can mean drought, failed harvests, water shortages and more wildfires.

variables.notes: POWER's IMERG_PRECTOT has no monthly data - use Giovanni for GPM.
variables.demo: Sahel rainy season Jul-Sep (12-15N, 5W-5E): POWER 1981-2025 +0.41 mm/day per decade (+37%), p=2e-5. Cross-check 2001-2025: POWER +0.73 vs GPM +0.35 mm/day per decade (MK p=0.07), year-to-year r=0.82.

variables.name: Snowfall
variables.plain: How much snow falls, measured as the water it would melt into.

story.name: Snowfall
story.why: How much snow falls, measured as the water it holds once melted. In mountain regions snow is a natural reservoir that feeds rivers through spring and summer.
story.up: More snowfall can refill mountain water supplies, but also raises avalanche risk.
story.down: Less snowfall means less river water in summer for drinking, farming and hydropower, and shorter snow seasons.

variables.name: Snow cover fraction
variables.plain: What share of the land is covered by snow.

story.name: Snow cover
story.why: How much of the ground is covered by snow (0 = none, 1 = all). White snow reflects most sunlight back to space, keeping the region cool.
story.up: More snow cover reflects more sunlight and keeps the area colder for longer.
story.down: Less snow uncovers darker ground that soaks up sunlight, which warms the region further. Plants and animals that rely on snow lose their season.

look.note: The map is MODIS satellite snow cover; the numbers are MERRA-2 (via POWER).

variables.demo: Alps Dec-Apr (45.5-47.5N, 7-12E): -0.023 per decade (~-25%), p=0.03 - significant but borderline

variables.name: Snow depth / snow water
variables.plain: How deep the snowpack is (or how much water is stored in it) - a water bank for spring rivers.

story.name: Snow depth
story.why: How much snow is lying on the ground. It melts in spring to feed rivers, soils and reservoirs.
story.up: Deeper snow stores more water for later in the year, but can cause floods if it melts fast.
story.down: Thinner snow means less meltwater in the dry season for drinking water, farms and hydropower.

variables.name: Sea ice cover
variables.plain: How much of the sea surface is frozen over.

story.name: Sea ice
story.why: The frozen ocean surface near the poles. Bright ice reflects most sunlight, while dark open water absorbs it. Polar bears, seals and walruses depend on it.
story.up: More sea ice reflects more sunlight and gives ice-dependent wildlife more room.
story.down: Less sea ice exposes dark ocean that absorbs more sunlight, which warms the poles even faster. It shrinks the habitat of polar bears and seals and changes life for Arctic communities.

convert.text: The ice lost covers an area about {x} times the size of Egypt.

access.source: Monthly concentration maps for time-lapse frames

access.period: 2012-07-02 to 2025-09-01 (AMSR-E layer ends 2011-10-04: 9-month gap, avoid for time-lapse)

variables.demo: Barents Sea (74-78N, 32-42E): -5 percentage points per decade, p=1e-6. Arctic September extent 6.25 M km2 (2000) -> 4.81 (2026), record low 3.57 (2012); -0.74 M km2/decade since 1979 (p=2e-17); since 2000 Sen -0.61/decade, MK p=0.0006
variables.notes: Floating sea ice melting does NOT raise sea level. Ice on land (ice sheets, glaciers) does - see ice_sheet_mass.

variables.name: Ice sheet mass (Greenland, Antarctica)
variables.plain: How much ice the giant land ice sheets have gained or lost, weighed from space by measuring tiny changes in gravity.

story.why: The ice piled up on land in Greenland or Antarctica, in gigatonnes (1 Gt = 1 billion tonnes). Melted land ice flows into the sea: about 360 Gt raises sea level everywhere by 1 mm.
story.up: Gaining ice would slightly lower sea level.
story.down: Losing ice raises sea level on every coast in the world, so storm surges and high tides flood more often.

convert.text: That melted ice alone has raised global sea level by about {x} mm.

access.source: GRACE + GRACE-FO, text file (time, Gt, 1-sigma Gt)
Global 0.5 deg grid of water/ice mass change, one 44 MB netCDF - time-lapse frames

access.period: 2002-04 to 2022-07 only (stale - make our own frames)

variables.demo: Greenland -6,086 Gt (Apr 2002 - Sep 2026, -255 Gt/yr, Hamed-Rao MK p=1e-5) = 16.8 mm of global sea level. Antarctica -2,492 Gt (-126 Gt/yr) = 6.9 mm
variables.notes: 362 Gt of ice = 1 mm global sea level. Gap Jul 2017 - May 2018 between GRACE and GRACE-FO: show it, never interpolate. Cite doi:10.5067/TEMSC-3JC634.

variables.name: Global mean sea level
variables.plain: How high the ocean surface is on average across the whole planet, measured by satellites bouncing radar off the sea.

story.name: Sea level
story.why: The average height of the world's oceans, measured by satellites. It rises because seawater expands as it warms and because melting land ice adds water. A higher sea lets every storm surge and high tide reach further inland.
story.up: Higher seas mean more coastal flooding, beaches washing away, and salt water reaching rivers, farmland and wells. Low islands and coastal cities are most at risk.
story.down: Falling seas would mean less coastal flooding.

convert.text: The whole ocean surface is now about {x} cm higher.

access.source: TOPEX/Jason/Sentinel-6 GMSL; column 12 = smoothed, GIA applied, seasons removed
Gridded sea surface height, ~1 MB per 5-day granule - only for a sea-level MAP

variables.demo: +84 mm from 2000 to May 2025 (v5.2). Rate 2.5 mm/yr in 2000-2010, 4.5 mm/yr in 2010-2020; quadratic fit acceleration 0.075 mm/yr^2
variables.notes: 8 cm is invisible as coastline change on a globe - show it as a gauge + chart, never as fake flooded coasts. Short windows mislead (2015-2026 fit = 3.6 mm/yr because of the 2015-16 El Nino bump). Cite doi:10.5067/GMSLM-TJ152.

variables.name: Evapotranspiration
variables.plain: Water returning to the air: evaporation from soil and water plus 'sweating' from plant leaves.

story.name: Water rising from land and plants
story.why: Water evaporating from soil and lakes plus water 'breathed out' by plant leaves. It shows how hard the land is working, and how fast it is drying out.
story.up: More evaporation dries soils faster, so crops need more water, though it can also mean plants are growing more.
story.down: Less evaporation can mean the soil has run out of water, a sign of drought, or that plants are struggling.

variables.name: Root-zone soil moisture
variables.plain: How wet the soil is down where plant roots drink (top ~1 m). Low = drought stress.

story.name: Water in the soil
story.why: How wet the soil is down to where plant roots reach (about 1 m). It decides whether crops and forests have enough water between rains.
story.up: Wetter soil helps crops and forests but raises flood and landslide risk.
story.down: Drier soil stresses crops and forests, lowers harvests and raises wildfire risk.

variables.demo: Arizona (32-35N, 113-110W): -8% since 1981, p=0.002 (megadrought). Interior Spain: no significant trend (p=0.45)

variables.name: Surface soil moisture
variables.plain: How wet the top few centimetres of soil are. Reacts quickly to rain and heat.

story.name: Water in the topsoil
story.why: How wet the top few centimetres of soil are. It reacts quickly to rain and heat and decides whether seeds can sprout.
story.up: Wetter topsoil helps seeds sprout and keeps dust down, but very wet ground floods more easily.
story.down: Drier topsoil makes planting harder, lets wind blow dust away, and is an early sign of drought.

variables.name: Runoff (streamflow proxy)
variables.plain: Water that flows off or through the land into streams and rivers instead of soaking in or evaporating.
variables.notes: Challenge mentions streamflow; GLDAS runoff is the global stand-in. For real gauges see CUAHSI HydroShare/USGS (non-NASA).

variables.name: Groundwater storage
variables.plain: How much water is stored underground, measured by satellites that weigh the Earth (GRACE).

variables.name: Vegetation greenness (NDVI)
variables.plain: A satellite 'greenness score' - higher means more, healthier green plants.

access.source: MODIS Terra MOD13Q1 v061 (250 m, 16-day) via ORNL DAAC, no login

variables.demo: Rondonia near Ariquemes (10.5-9.5S, 63.5-62.5W), MOD13A3 via AppEEARS (48 min): dry-season Jul-Sep NDVI 0.725 -> 0.595, -0.049/decade, p<1e-6; wet season no trend (p=0.59) - the trend hides in one season.

variables.name: Burned area
variables.plain: How much land burned in fires each month.

access.source: MODIS monthly 500 m; count pixels with Burn_Date > 0

variables.name: Surface albedo (reflectivity)
variables.plain: How much sunlight the surface bounces back. Snow is bright (high), forests and oceans are dark (low).

story.name: How much sunlight the ground reflects
story.why: The share of sunlight bounced straight back to space (0 = all absorbed, 1 = all reflected). Snow and ice reflect a lot; forests, oceans and dark soil much less.
story.up: A more reflective surface absorbs less sunlight, which tends to cool the area. It can mean more snow or a change in what covers the land.
story.down: A darker surface absorbs more sunlight and warms up. Melting snow and ice is the most common cause, and it speeds up warming.

variables.name: Aerosol optical depth (haze)
variables.plain: How hazy the air is - smoke, dust and pollution particles that block sunlight. 0.1 = clean, above 0.5 = very hazy.

story.name: Haze in the air
story.why: How much dust, smoke and pollution in the air dims sunlight (around 0.1 is clear air, above 1 is very hazy).
story.up: More haze means dirtier air to breathe, which harms lungs and hearts, and less sunlight at the ground. It often comes from fires, dust storms or pollution.
story.down: Less haze usually means cleaner air, often thanks to pollution controls, and a little more sunlight reaching the ground.

variables.demo: Eastern China: rose 2001-2011 (+0.17/decade) then fell 2012-2025 (-0.26/decade) after clean-air policy. Indo-Gangetic Plain: +0.086/decade, p=1e-11

variables.name: Dust in the air
variables.plain: How much desert dust is suspended in the air above a place.

variables.name: Nitrogen dioxide (NO2) pollution
variables.plain: A gas from car exhausts, power plants and industry. Satellites map it from space.

variables.name: Sulfur dioxide (SO2)
variables.plain: A gas from burning coal and from volcanoes.

variables.name: Total ozone
variables.plain: The ozone layer that shields us from UV. The Antarctic 'ozone hole' opens every Sep-Oct.

look.note: The map shows ozone at 50 hPa (~20 km up, inside the ozone layer).

variables.notes: POWER TO3 has gaps at polar latitudes (polar night) - do not use for Antarctica.

variables.name: UV index
variables.plain: How strong sunburn-causing ultraviolet light is.

story.name: UV index
story.why: How strong the Sun's sunburn-causing ultraviolet light is. 0 to 2 is low; 8 and above is very high, when unprotected skin burns quickly.
story.up: Stronger UV raises the risk of sunburn, skin cancer and eye damage. Clearer skies or a thinner ozone layer can cause it.
story.down: Weaker UV usually means more cloud or haze. A recovering ozone layer also helps.

look.note: The map is the CERES monthly UV index, which NASA only publishes as a map for 2002–2021.

variables.name: Carbon dioxide (column average)
variables.plain: The main heat-trapping gas from burning fossil fuels, averaged through the whole atmosphere.
variables.notes: Rises everywhere (~2.4 ppm/yr): good 'obviously significant' calibration example.

variables.name: Global temperature anomaly
variables.plain: How much warmer or cooler the whole planet is than its 1951-1980 average.

story.name: Average temperature
story.why: The temperature of the whole planet compared with the 1951–1980 average. Small numbers matter here: the last Ice Age was only about 6 °C colder than the 1800s.
story.up: A warmer planet brings more heatwaves, heavier downpours, rising seas, melting ice, and seasons shifting for plants and animals.
story.down: A cooler planet would bring fewer heat extremes.

look.note: The map shows air temperature; the numbers are the whole-planet anomaly (GISTEMP).

variables.notes: Context strip for every chart: 'the globe warmed X in the same period'.
